articleHeadline: Lab experiments suggest bat RSV can enter human cells, but existing antibodies block it
articleSummary: West African fruit bat RSV, genetically distinct from human RSV, was characterized by researchers led by Dr. Jo and Dr. Drexler at Charité, Berlin, and colleagues at TWINCORE, Hanover. Fieldwork on 1,778 bats from Ghana and Benin found a 1.4% virus detection rate and RSV-like antibodies in 9% of bats. Genomic analyses show these bat RSVs are not closely related to human RSV, yet experiments demonstrate the virus can enter human cells, less efficiently than human RSV. Bat RSV can suppress the human innate immune response but is neutralized by antibodies from RSV-exposed individuals, and a broadly effective monoclonal antibody also neutralizes bat RSV. The study notes the importance of combining genomic and functional data to assess zoonotic risk and supports the development of broad-spectrum antivirals. No human cases reported; next steps use reverse genetics to study pathogenesis.
notes: 本記事はコウモリ由来RSVの実験室研究（ドイツ・ガーナ・ベナンでのフィールドワークを含む）であり、人獣共通感染症リスクの基礎評価にとどまる。ヒト症例は報告されておらず、ガーナ・ベナンも『発生地域』としては不適切（実際の人への感染事例ではなくサンプル採取地のため）。ドイツは対象国リストに含まれず、ガーナ・ベナンも感染イベントの主題ではないため verified_locations は空とした。

articleHeadline: Automated Urine Assay Improves Paediatric Tuberculosis Detection in
articleSummary: Automated PATHFAST TB LAM Ag urine chemiluminescent immunoassay detected 83% of microbiologically confirmed TB cases in HIV-infected, and 67% in HIV-uninfected hospitalized children with presumptive TB in Zambia, outperforming Determine TB-LAM and an in-house IS6110 urine PCR on the same samples. The urine sub-study (PROMISE-TB) analyzed 339 children at University Teaching Hospital, Lusaka, and Arthur Davison Children’s Hospital, Ndola, using archived urine collected 2013–2015; 63 had microbiologically confirmed TB, 276 were negative on respiratory testing. Context highlights extensive pediatric TB diagnostic gaps per WHO TB Report 2025, with ~52% of under-fives undiagnosed and 1.2 million cases and 172,000 deaths in 2024. LAM is a non-invasive biomarker; WHO guidance centers Determine LAM for hospitalized adults and HIV‑positive children, while newer urine assays show variable sensitivity. PATHFAST’s higher sensitivity with preserved specificity suggests potential for improving pediatric TB detection in low-resource settings.
